controls.label: Monochrome
controls.filter: MESSENGER MDIS BDR global 750 nm monochrome basemap
controls.notes: MESSENGER MDIS BDR, edition 1 (2016). Images were selected with the Sun about 16° above the local horizon to show terrain. USGS corrected reflectance and stretched 0.0005–0.25 I/F into this 8-bit display image. Brightness is not directly comparable with the higher-Sun map. Native spacing is about 166 m; the display is reduced to 4,096 pixels around the equator. Gray grid marks missing source coverage.

controls.label: Monochrome
controls.filter: MESSENGER MDIS LOI global monochrome basemap
controls.notes: MESSENGER MDIS LOI, edition 1 (2016). Images were selected with the Sun about 45° above the local horizon. USGS corrected reflectance and stretched 0.005–about 0.2 I/F into this 8-bit display image. Brightness is not directly comparable with the low-Sun map. Native spacing is about 166 m; the display is reduced to 4,096 pixels around the equator. Gray grid marks missing source coverage.

controls.label: Color
controls.filter: USGS MESSENGER MDIS native MD3 color mosaic
controls.notes: USGS MD3 color mosaic, edition 1 (2016), from MESSENGER's 3-color map campaign. Red, green and blue are the 1000, 750 and 430 nm filter images. Each was corrected to 30° incidence, 0° emission and 30° phase, and USGS stretched about 0–0.2 reflectance into 8 bits. Each pixel averages every image that met the scale, lighting and detector-temperature criteria. 1000 nm is beyond human vision, so these are not the colors an eye would see. Native spacing is about 665 m; the display is reduced to 4,096 pixels around the equator. Gray grid marks missing coverage, including the polar gaps.

controls.label: Enhanced
controls.filter: USGS MESSENGER MDIS native enhanced-color mosaic
controls.notes: USGS enhanced-color mosaic, edition 1 (2016). Red is principal component 2, green is principal component 1, and blue is the 430/1000 nm ratio. These colors emphasize differences in the surface; they are not natural colors or a map of specific minerals. Native spacing is about 665 m; the display is reduced to 4,096 pixels around the equator. Gray grid marks missing coverage, including the polar gaps. No color is reconstructed there.

controls.label: Elevation
controls.qualification: USGS MESSENGER global DEM v2 (2016), with native spacing about 665 m. Heights are meters above a 2,439.4 km sphere. USGS interpolated and smoothed the image-derived control-point cloud after a one-sigma filter. This display uses the numeric DEM with its own matching color scale.
controls.notes: Mercury has no sea level. Heights use a reference sphere with a radius of 2,439.4 km; zero means the surface of that sphere. Meters above the reference sphere. Blue is lower and warm colors are higher; values beyond −6,000 or +6,000 m use endpoint colors. USGS matched surface points across MESSENGER images to build its 2016 global elevation model, version 2. The source spacing is about 665 m. The height model was filtered, smoothed and interpolated; this globe displays a coarser sample. Gray grid marks missing source data.

controls.label: Gravity
controls.qualification: MESSENGER gravity model HgM008 (Genova et al. 2019), free-air gravity anomaly to degree 90, from the NASA Goddard grid published by NASA Mercury Trek. Values are mGal at a 2,440 km reference radius.
controls.notes: How much Mercury’s gravity differs from the pull of a perfectly round, evenly dense planet, at a radius of 2,440 km. Extra mass below the surface pulls harder. Milligals (mGal): 1 mGal is 0.00001 m/s², and Mercury’s surface gravity is about 370,000 mGal. Red pulls harder and blue weaker; values beyond −150 or +150 mGal use endpoint colors. NASA Goddard’s HgM008 gravity model (Genova et al. 2019) comes from radio tracking of the MESSENGER spacecraft, 2008–2015. This map adds its terms up to degree 90. Detail depends on how low MESSENGER flew. The model resolves features about 105–125 km across near the north pole, but only about 500–700 km across south of 30° S. Southern patterns are broad because they are not resolved.

controls.label: Crust
controls.qualification: Crustal-thickness model of Genova et al. (2019) from HgM008 gravity and MESSENGER laser-altimeter topography, degrees 2–60; crust 2,800 kg/m³, crust–mantle density contrast 400 kg/m³, mean thickness 35 km. Grid published by NASA Mercury Trek.
controls.notes: Estimated depth from the surface to the bottom of the rocky crust, in kilometers. It is a model, not a measurement. Kilometers. Purple is thinner and yellow is thicker; values below 0 or above 70 km use endpoint colors. Genova et al. (2019) combined the HgM008 gravity model with MESSENGER laser-altimeter heights. They assumed a crust density of 2,800 kg/m³, a mantle 400 kg/m³ denser, and an average thickness of 35 km, using degrees 2 to 60. Other densities or another average thickness give a different map. Detail follows the gravity model: finer in the north, coarse in the south. Under Rachmaninoff basin the model falls slightly below zero, to −3 km, which is not physical.
